passage: The evening bus was packed and steamy with rain, and Sabina was wedged against a pole with her bag clutched to her chest. Someone behind her pressed closer each time the bus braked, and when she shifted away, he followed. His hand brushed her back again. Her heart was pounding, and under the fear she felt a hot spike of anger. "Stop. Move away," she said loudly, turning to face him. Nobody spoke, but a few heads turned. She pushed through to the front, where Bhupen the conductor was collecting tickets. "That man behind me won't stop," she said. Bhupen looked back, rang the bell and called out, "This man gets off at the next stop." The next morning Sabina wrote down the bus number and gave it to the campus women's committee. She was still shaking, but she knew it was not her fault.

qa.q: Who did Sabina tell at the front of the bus?
What was Sabina feeling when she told the man to stop?
qa.a: She felt fear with a hot spike of anger. Her heart was pounding, but she still said it loudly.

qa.q: Which of Sabina's steps are worth repeating?
qa.a: She said a firm no, moved towards staff, and reported it the next morning with the bus number. She can also tell a friend or warden. 🤍

qa.q: How might Bhupen the conductor have seen the moment?
qa.a: Bhupen seems to have taken her seriously, since Bhupen looked back at the man and announced that he must get off. A rider speaking up lets the conductor protect the other passengers too.

grounding: A stranger will not stop unwanted advances on a bus; the protagonist says a firm no, moves away, reports it, and knows it is not her fault.

passage:
Rain hammered the windows of the 9:40 bus to Kothrud, and every seat was full. Avni stood holding the rail when the man behind her pressed closer than the crowd required.
She shifted. He shifted too.
"Move back," she said, loud enough for the nearby row to hear. "Right now."
He smirked. "Bus is crowded, madam."
"Then stand somewhere else." Her voice shook, but she didn't lower it. She squeezed forward to the conductor. "That man in the grey jacket keeps pushing against me."
The conductor turned. "You. Get down at the next stop." Two women nodded at Avni.
Her phone was at four percent. She called Vasudha, her hostel roommate. "I'm okay. Meet me at the stop?"
Vasudha was waiting under an umbrella. That night, together, they wrote to the women's helpline and the warden with the bus number and time. "It's not on you," Vasudha said. "Not one bit."

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she said "Move back"?
qa.a: Scared and angry, since her voice shook, but determined not to lower it.

qa.q: Which of Avni's steps kept her safer?
qa.a: A firm, loud no, moving next to the conductor and reporting the man, calling Vasudha, and writing to the helpline and warden with the bus number and time.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see what happened?
qa.a: As entirely the man's doing, not Avni's fault, so she waits with an umbrella and helps report it.

grounding: Shows unwanted advances from a stranger on a bus and the response of a firm no, moving away, reporting, and being told it is not her fault.

passage:
For two weeks, a man from the third floor of Rafiq's paying-guest building in Hyderabad had been finding reasons to talk to him: at the water cooler, on the stairs, outside the bathroom. Then the messages started. "You look good today." "Come to my room, we'll chill." Rafiq replied once: "Not interested. Please stop." The next morning there was a note under his door.
Rafiq told no one at first. It felt ridiculous, a grown guy scared to walk down a corridor. He started showering at odd hours to avoid it.
On Friday, Sharmila, who managed the building, noticed him taking the long staircase again. "Everything okay, Rafiq?"
He showed her the messages and the note. She read them slowly, then looked up. "Thank you for telling me. This isn't your fault. Save everything and block him now. I'm speaking to him today, and if it continues, he leaves."
By evening, the man's number was blocked and he had a written warning from the management.

qa.q: Where did the man find reasons to talk to Rafiq?
qa.a: At the water cooler, on the stairs and outside the bathroom.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq start showering at odd hours?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and embarrassed, so he tried to avoid the man instead of telling anyone.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that helped?
qa.a: She thanked Rafiq, said it wasn't his fault, told him to save everything and block the man, spoke to the man that day and gave a written warning.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see Rafiq's report?
qa.a: As a serious problem in her building, not something ridiculous, and she acts on it the same day.

grounding: Illustrates unwanted advances from a stranger in a hostel-like building, a firm no, and reporting to the person in charge; it is not the target's fault.
